video_title: The Warehouse War - The "Wildberries" Strikes, Economics & Russian Response
gist: Perun argues Ukraine's July-August 2026 drone campaign against Wildberries (Russia's Amazon analog) warehouses is not a substitution for its refinery, shipping and logistics strikes but an addition enabled by scaling one-way attack drone output — and that its real payoff is financial: injecting risk into an already-strained Russian corporate debt market where Wildberries carries ~$11bn of debt owed largely to state-linked VTB. He quantifies the damage (roughly 900k-1.15m m2 of warehouse space hit, $2.2bn rebuild cost, seller stock losses revised up to ~$5.7bn) against a Russian macro backdrop of 2.8%-of-GDP deficits in seven months, 14% policy rates, suspended OFZ auctions and ~12% problematic corporate loans, then argues Russia's mirror strikes on Ukrainian warehouses are a poor use of scarce Iskanders and jet drones.

insights.claim: Ukraine's strikes on Russian e-commerce warehouses are an added target category rather than a reallocation away from refineries, logistics and shipping, which all continued or accelerated over the same period.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Do not read warehouse-strike headlines as a de-escalation of pressure on Russian refining or export capacity; the refinery-driven crude and product supply risk premium stays intact.

insights.claim: The expansion of Ukraine's target set is funded by raw drone output: one-way attack drone launches by Ukraine have risen sharply while Russian long-range drone attacks have slightly declined, per strike-tracking data cited from Clement Molin.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Drone production capacity, not target-list scarcity, is now the binding constraint on Ukraine's deep-strike reach — watch Ukrainian UAV manufacturing scale as the leading indicator of new target categories.

insights.claim: Russia's declining long-range drone count masks a mix shift, not a decline in effort: ballistic missile attacks are up and Russia is transitioning from propeller-driven Shahed-type drones to faster, harder-to-intercept but more expensive and slower-to-produce jet-powered variants.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Falling Russian drone launch counts should not be scored as reduced threat; interception economics for Ukraine get worse as the mix moves to jet drones and ballistic missiles.

insights.claim: Cross-checking adversary claims is a reliable way to filter propaganda: when Ukraine claims more launches and Russia claims more shoot-downs, the trend of more drones can be treated as real even if the absolute numbers are unreliable.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: A reusable filter for war-data investing: trust the direction where both hostile sources agree, discount the levels either side reports.

insights.claim: Russian state media's failure to claim Black Sea shipping is safe — instead emphasising ~$1bn of Ukrainian FX losses from the blockade begun 22 July — is itself evidence Ukraine has not eased its anti-shipping campaign.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Adversary messaging omissions are a tradeable tell on which side believes it is winning a given attrition sub-campaign.

themes.theme: Refinery attrition and Russian fuel economics

insights.claim: Russian refineries processed an estimated 3.6 million barrels per day in July 2026, the lowest monthly level cited since May 2002, against a 2020-2025 average of 5.3 to 5.6 million barrels per day, per analysis attributed to Bloomberg.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: A ~1.7-2.0 mb/d hole in Russian refining runs means more crude pushed to export and structurally tighter global product cracks — a direct diesel and gasoline crack spread trade.

insights.claim: The tempo of Ukrainian refinery strikes accelerated from roughly one target every two days in July 2026 to closer to one per day in the first week of August, with a claimed 18 refineries struck in a month breaking the prior record of 17 set in May.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Strike cadence is still rising, so Russian throughput has not yet found a floor; position for continued downside to Russian refining runs into Q4.

insights.claim: A refinery near Omsk roughly 1,500 km from the front line was damaged so severely that Russian authorities themselves acknowledged the facility is offline and may remain so for about six months.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Depth of reach plus six-month outages means Ukrainian strikes now impose semi-permanent, not temporary, capacity loss deep inside Russia.

insights.claim: The damage extends beyond motor fuels: one of Russia's largest recently struck and offlined complexes reportedly produced around 40% of the country's LPG.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Watch Russian LPG export volumes and domestic petrochemical feedstock prices as an under-covered second-order casualty of the refinery campaign.

insights.claim: Russia's partial fuel-supply recovery — larger retailers such as Gazprom lifting purchase restrictions in some regions — reflects adaptation (becoming a frantic product importer, cutting fuel standards, prioritising allocation) rather than any let-up in Ukrainian strikes.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Normalising Russian pump availability is a misleading all-clear; the underlying refining deficit persists and shows up as import demand and degraded fuel quality instead.

insights.claim: Refinery output should be modelled as a race between repair rate and destruction rate rather than a one-way decline, implying bumpy, mean-reverting monthly data even while the campaign intensifies.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Do not fade the thesis on a single month of recovering Russian runs; judge the campaign on multi-month trend, not print-to-print noise.
insights.quote: It's more this is a race between constant regeneration and pace of destruction and the balance between those two can absolutely tip back and forth.

insights.claim: Breaking down a country's refining sector requires years of repeated restrikes: Russian refining fell in 2024 versus 2023 and again in 2025, but only in 2026 after sustained persistence did volumes drop sharply, echoing post-WWII strategic bombing studies.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Cumulative-attrition targets have convex payoffs late in the campaign — the marginal strike in 2026 is worth far more than in 2024, which also makes any pause disproportionately costly.

themes.theme: Risk as the weapon: shipping and logistics paralysis

insights.claim: Maritime traffic to Russian Black Sea ports has collapsed even as claimed strike counts fall: July tanker calls at Novorossiysk were down about 50% and grain carriers 46%, with Sea of Azov traffic a fraction of former levels.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Fewer claimed hits reflects target scarcity, not restored safety — Russian seaborne crude and grain export logistics remain structurally impaired and freight/insurance costs elevated.

insights.claim: A large-scale Ukrainian attack on Novorossiysk, Russia's nominal safe harbour on the Black Sea, scored multiple hits and per Reuters forced Russia to suspend some crude oil exports from the port.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Export-terminal outages, not just refinery outages, are now a live tail risk for Russian crude flows and Urals differentials.

insights.claim: Injected risk destroys far more economic activity than the ordnance itself, because every counterparty in the market either prices a premium or refuses to hold the exposure.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Size the economic impact of strike campaigns by the risk premium they create across the whole market, not the replacement cost of what burned.
insights.quote: The Iranians hit a couple of ships. They paralyze hundreds. The Ukrainians burn down 10 digits worth of warehouse value. They might do 11 digits worth of total economic damage.

insights.claim: Ukraine's mid-range campaign against Russian frontline logistics keeps growing — visually confirmed truck strikes tracked by Clement Molin were higher in July than June — and Russian counter-drone convoy escorts with EW, autocannons and MANPADS have not stopped the losses.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Russian frontline supply costs are rising continuously; absence of an improvement in Russian supply conditions is corroborating evidence the campaign is biting.

themes.theme: Wildberries: anatomy of an ideal soft target

insights.claim: Wildberries is Russia's largest e-commerce firm and roughly tripled sales from 2021 to 2023 while capex exploded — up about 85% in 2023 to 52bn rubles, tripling in 2024 to 150bn, and doubling again in 2025 to north of 300bn rubles (over $3.5bn) — making it a pillar of what the Kremlin calls the platform economy.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: The debt-funded capex boom that made Wildberries systemically important is exactly what makes its warehouse footprint a concentrated, leveraged point of failure.

insights.claim: Wildberries was a direct beneficiary of sanctions-era restructuring, supplying parallel-import goods and openly marketing a searchable 'for the special military operation' product category covering helmets, plate carriers and drone components until it was quietly removed after the strikes began.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: The company's role in the sanctioned-component supply chain gives Ukraine a defensible legal-military justification for a target whose real value is economic.

insights.claim: Ukraine opened the warehouse campaign against the biggest and best-defended sites first — a 230,000 m2 facility at Elektrostal and a 100,000 m2 site on 18 July, then a 250,000 m2 Moscow-region facility on 20 July — before spreading to smaller regional targets.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Surprise was deliberately spent on the highest-value, best-defended nodes first — a pattern to expect when Ukraine opens any future new target category.

insights.claim: E-commerce mega-warehouses are near-ideal drone targets because they concentrate enormous value in structures optimised purely for cost efficiency, with stacked cardboard and plastic providing most of the destructive energy and little visible firefighting capability.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Any operator of large, cheaply built, high-value-density logistics real estate within drone range now carries an uninsured tail risk — a template applicable well beyond Russia.
insights.quote: if you so much tickle this thing, you are going to get an enormous self-perpetuating incendiary event

insights.claim: Ukraine's arsenal split — vast numbers of slow one-way attack drones with warheads of 100 kg or less versus a small number of vulnerable Flamingo cruise missiles — means its scarce resource is destructive power per munition, so it needs targets a small warhead can finish.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Predict Ukraine's next target categories by asking which assets are both valuable and destroyable by a sub-100 kg warhead; hardened factories will keep resisting drone attack.

insights.claim: Russia is committing some of its rarest assets — remaining A-50 AWACS aircraft and Su-57 fighters — to defending key facilities against Flamingo cruise missile attack.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Even a handful of credible Ukrainian cruise missiles ties down disproportionately scarce Russian high-end air assets — a cheap asymmetric return on a small missile inventory.

insights.claim: Adding hundreds of dispersed warehouse targets stretches a Russian air defence network already concentrated in multiple rings around Moscow, mechanically raising leakage rates against every other target type.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: The warehouse campaign's biggest payoff may be indirect: higher penetration rates on refineries and export terminals as air defence thins out elsewhere.

insights.claim: Even heavily defended Moscow-area sites are not safe: as the episode was being edited, one of Wildberries' largest previously undamaged facilities at roughly 250,000 m2 near Moscow was struck.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Proximity to Moscow's air defence rings is no longer a reliable insurance policy for Russian commercial real estate.

themes.theme: The contagion thesis: warehouses as a debt pinata

insights.claim: Ukrainian sources frame Wildberries as a leveraged target whose ~$11bn equivalent of reported debt, much owed to partly state-owned VTB, only stays serviceable while the revenues that debt financed keep flowing.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: The strike campaign is effectively a short position on a levered Russian corporate borrower and its state-linked creditor — watch VTB disclosures and Wildberries restructuring news.
insights.quote: Wildbears is essentially a very flammable debt pinata.

insights.claim: The intended mechanism is contagion: destroyed inventory wipes out often unincorporated, personally liable third-party sellers, whose defaults threaten business loans and mortgages and then propagate to suppliers, distributors, logistics partners and lenders.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: The credit impairment channel, not the physical damage, is where the multiplier lives — watch Russian SME NPL data and consumer loan delinquency for confirmation.

insights.claim: Insurance offers Russian e-commerce sellers almost no protection: Wildberries and Ozon have raised seller insurance costs to between 1.96% and 5.6% of item value at Wildberries, yet cover for a Ukrainian drone strike or sabotage is reportedly only about $1,200 per incident.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Losses fall on sellers' balance sheets rather than being mutualised through insurers, maximising default risk and making the contagion path more, not less, likely.
insights.quote: As far as a lot of insurance policies go, Ukrainian drone strike is going to fall into the not my problem category.

insights.claim: Estimated direct damage as of early August was roughly $2.2bn to rebuild destroyed Wildberries sites with 900,000 to 1.15 million m2 of warehouse space affected, and seller stock losses initially put at $2.7-3.5bn by Forbes were later revised up to around $5.7bn in New York Times reporting.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Damage estimates are being revised upward faster than the strikes are reported — assume published loss figures lag reality by weeks.

insights.claim: There is highly unconfirmed reporting that Wildberries approached the Kremlin for roughly $10bn of support combining seller compensation and air defence systems for its remaining facilities.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: If true, the ask exceeds direct damage estimates several times over and would set a precedent for privately funded point air defence around Russian commercial assets.

insights.claim: VTB shares, the bank specifically named by Ukrainian officials as Wildberries' creditor, are down about 31% over twelve months and about 14% in the last month.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: A partly state-owned bank's falling share price reduces its capacity to raise capital, tightening credit supply and creating a self-reinforcing deposit-flight risk.

insights.claim: VTB signalled in late July it would consider credit support for the Wildberries and Russ Group if asked, which Perun frames as the classic creditor trap of rescuing a primary debtor rather than letting it fail.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Expect a quiet bank-led bailout rather than a visible corporate default — the loss migrates onto state-linked bank balance sheets instead of showing up as a headline bankruptcy.
insights.quote: if you owe a bank 100 bucks, that's your problem. But if you owe the bank 100 million, that's the bank's problem.

insights.claim: Russia can absorb the current level of damage, but it only gets to choose where the loss sits — on the state budget, on state-owned bank balance sheets, or on companies and the wider economy through knock-on effects.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Track which balance sheet absorbs each shock: state absorption suppresses visible contagion but accelerates fiscal and inflationary strain instead.

insights.claim: Because the warehouse campaign was a low-cost side quest for Ukraine's long-range strike effort, the cost-to-inflict versus cost-to-manage ratio can justify it even if the strikes are never strategically decisive.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Evaluate deep-strike campaigns on economic exchange ratio rather than on whether they change the war's outcome — by that metric this one likely continues.

insights.claim: Russia's budget deficit reached about 2.8% of GDP for January through July 2026 against a full-year target of roughly 1.6%, a ~17% increase on the same period of 2025 despite non-oil-and-gas revenues and taxes rising about 18% year on year.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Fiscal headroom for bailing out the e-commerce sector is shrinking fast; any Wildberries rescue implies cuts elsewhere or monetary financing.
insights.quote: So from a budget perspective, that spoonful of stimulus sugar has become a shovel.

insights.claim: Russia's central bank has cut its 2026 GDP growth projection to between zero and 0.5% while raising its inflation forecast to 6.5-7%, with the policy rate at 14% and borrowers demanding cuts they cannot get without stoking inflation.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Stagflationary squeeze plus a 14% policy rate means Russian corporate borrowers have no refinancing relief coming, amplifying any strike-induced credit shock.

insights.claim: Russian loan quality is visibly deteriorating: Sberbank warned in July of worsening loan book quality, the central bank classified roughly 12% of corporate and 13% of consumer loans as problematic as at early June totalling 167 billion, and Sberbank reports about 5.12% of its own loans as non-performing.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: The Russian banking system is entering the warehouse shock with already-elevated problem loans — the buffer for a seller-default wave is thinner than headline stability suggests.

insights.claim: Russia's Ministry of Finance officially suspended domestic bond auctions last month after several failed auctions in which banks refused to buy OFZ at the offered rates, with Sberbank's CFO citing a liquidity shortage after roughly $2bn of cash withdrawals from the banking system since the start of the year.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: With international bond markets closed by sanctions and domestic auctions suspended, Russia's only remaining funding levers are spending cuts or covert monetisation.
insights.quote: Today, banks only have enough funds to lend to customers. That is their core business.

insights.claim: The failed OFZ auctions expose an absurdity of Russia's state-dominated financial system in which a state-owned bank declines to fund the state so it can keep lending to private borrowers.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: State ownership does not guarantee funding capacity — the constraint is real liquidity, not political will, which limits Moscow's crisis-response toolkit.
insights.quote: the Russian government here is refusing to lend itself money so it can continue lending to other people instead

insights.claim: The likely funding workaround is what Ukrainian sources call indirect money printing: the central bank supplies liquidity to state banks via repo or similar facilities, those banks buy government bonds, and the state spends the proceeds — paying for the war with current or deferred inflation rather than hard currency.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Watch Bank of Russia repo volumes to state banks as the tell for covert deficit monetisation, and expect ruble and inflation expectations to be the transmission channel.

insights.claim: Under fractional reserve banking, the deposits pulled out of Russia's banking system tighten the credit market by a multiple of the withdrawn amount, so deposit flight compounds the strike-induced credit shock.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Deposit outflow data is a higher-leverage indicator of Russian credit stress than headline bank capital ratios.

insights.claim: Russia's increasing classification or cessation of publication of financial reserve data means outside observers have progressively less certainty about how Moscow could fund a major shock.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Rising data opacity should widen confidence intervals on Russian fiscal capacity — treat 'Russia can afford it' claims as increasingly unfalsifiable.

themes.theme: Russia's counter-strikes and the asymmetry of arsenals

insights.claim: Russia responded to the Wildberries campaign by dialling up strikes on Ukrainian commercial logistics, using missiles rather than just drones against targets including the home-improvement retailer Epicenter, while asserting the facilities stored dual-use goods and drone components.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Mirror-imaging on rhetoric masks a real difference in weapon cost per target — the symmetry is rhetorical, not economic.

insights.claim: The exchange is quantitatively lopsided: Ukraine has reportedly lost around 400,000 m2 of warehouse space to Russian attacks versus roughly three times that lost by Russia, and Ukrainian facilities such as Nova Poshta sorting centres are transit nodes rather than months-of-inventory storage.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Maximum economic damage per target struck is structurally lower in Ukraine, so tit-for-tat warehouse escalation favours Kyiv on the exchange ratio.

insights.claim: The argument that Ukraine erred by opening a target category because Russia retaliates in kind is flawed, since Russian munitions would otherwise be tasked against something else rather than not fired at all.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Judge escalation decisions by opportunity cost of the adversary's munitions, not by the visible pain of retaliation — a correction to a widespread commentary error.

insights.claim: Horizontal escalation into soft, dispersed targets structurally favours Ukraine because its problem is penetrating air defence with cheap slow drones, whereas Russia's problem is finding maximally valuable targets given it already penetrates Ukrainian defences.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Every Iskander or jet drone Russia spends on a Ukrainian warehouse is one not spent on a drone factory or air defence site — a net win for Ukraine's war economy.

insights.claim: With Patriot PAC-3 magazines exhausted and ballistic missile interception rates low, Ukraine's defensive posture against the Russian bombing campaign has effectively become absorption rather than denial.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Interceptor resupply is now the binding constraint on Ukrainian infrastructure survival — a key variable for Ukrainian reconstruction and energy risk this winter.
insights.quote: Ukraine's defense strategy against the Russian bombing campaign at this point is basically absorption.

insights.claim: Russian drone footage of post-strike battle damage assessment over Kyiv, recovered with a good enough data link for later release, is further evidence Ukraine's air defence net around the capital is not airtight against higher-end threats.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Russian ISR persistence over Kyiv implies improving Russian targeting quality, raising the expected damage per missile in coming strike waves.

themes.theme: Target diplomacy, ceasefire game theory and what comes next

insights.claim: Russia has underperformed at target diplomacy: it has repeatedly declined Ukrainian energy-ceasefire offers and has made no public attempt to propose warehouse targeting restrictions, despite arguably losing more from those strikes than Ukraine both directly and in munitions opportunity cost.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: A cheap de-escalation option Moscow keeps refusing signals either misjudgement or a preference for coercive pressure — lowering the odds of negotiated targeting restrictions.
insights.quote: working on peace in Ukraine, not a ceasefire

insights.claim: An energy ceasefire would be structurally asymmetric against Ukraine because refinery degradation requires years of cumulative restrikes that regenerate during any pause, while Ukraine's power grid is a seasonal target Russia can devastate quickly in winter after stockpiling missiles.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Any headline energy truce should be read as bullish Russian refining throughput and bearish Ukrainian winter grid resilience, not as symmetric relief.

insights.claim: The precedent already exists: a short energy ceasefire in early 2025 appears to have allowed Russia to stockpile munitions, followed by a surge in attacks on Ukrainian energy infrastructure once it lapsed.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Price ceasefire announcements as option value for the side with stockpilable munitions, and expect a post-truce attack surge rather than durable calm.

insights.claim: Perun expects warehouse strikes to continue but at a lower cadence, with periodic attacks used to keep Russian air defence tied down, disrupt the business model and maintain the perception of risk, and with the drones redirected elsewhere if penetration rates fall.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Expect maintenance-level rather than escalating strikes on Russian e-commerce; risk premia on Russian logistics assets stay elevated without new headline damage.

insights.claim: Neither side's strike campaign will force an end to the war before winter, with Zelensky himself conceding Putin hopes to drag the war out and no evidence Moscow is modifying its war goals.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Do not price a pre-winter ceasefire; plan around another Russian winter campaign against Ukrainian energy infrastructure.
insights.quote: We clearly understand who we are dealing with and that Putin hopes to continue dragging out this war.

insights.claim: Sabotage is a plausible next vector against warehouses, since both sides have recruited civilians for arson and one person with a bottle and a lighter is far cheaper than a drone against a structure that self-destructs once ignited.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Physical security and insurance underwriting for large logistics real estate in both countries should assume an arson threat that air defence cannot address.

insights.claim: Even if strikes stopped entirely, the permanent legacy is a higher cost structure: logistics networks reconfigured around smaller dispersed warehouses, higher insurance and lease premiums, and workarounds that persist until facilities are genuinely considered safe.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: The margin compression in Russian and Ukrainian e-commerce and logistics is a permanent war cost already baked in, independent of future strike cadence.

insights.claim: The campaign is a warning to any country dependent on extremely expensive, highly flammable mega-installations that can be destroyed by relatively small-scale attacks.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Cheap drones invert the economics of value-density in logistics real estate globally — a durable underwriting and siting risk for Western distribution networks too.

insights.claim: Pressuring an adversary's civilian population is historically an unreliable route to ending a war, as shown by Ukrainians enduring years of blackouts without a polling majority for the concessions Russia demands, even though the Kremlin's avoidance of full mobilisation shows it is somewhat sensitive to public opinion.
insights.speaker: Perun
insights.so_what: Discount the 'make Russians feel the war' rationale offered by Ukraine's unmanned systems commander; the economic-attrition and air-defence-stretching effects are the ones worth modelling.
insights.quote: Make ordinary Russians feel the war directly in the hope the resulting desire to end it could weigh on Russia's ability to keep fighting.
